Getting Started with Moosaic

moosaic-getting-started.Rmd

What moosaic does

moosaic turns raw GC-FID/MS data into a quantified compound report. If you have ever looked at a real run, the FID trace is a stack of partly overlapping peaks and every mass spectrum in the TIC is a blend of whatever is eluting at that moment – basic peak picking hands you apex times and areas for that tangle, not for the individual compounds inside it. moosaic untangles this: given the ChemStation files of one run – data.ms for the mass spectrometer and fid.ch for the FID – it aligns the two detectors, deconvolves each FID window into pure components by FID-constrained MCR-ALS, identifies the components against a NIST-format library with retention-index and element penalties, quantifies them by the Polyarc method, and writes Excel and PDF reports. The one-call entry point runs every stage:

read_experiment() -> align_detectors() -> deconvolve_run() -> identify_components() -> quantify() -> summarize_report()

A methods write-up covering the deconvolution and identification stages in depth is planned; this vignette gets you from raw data to a report file.

What you need

  • The ChemStation files of one run: an MS file (.ms) and its FID file (.ch). The two detectors see each peak a fraction of a minute apart, so moosaic needs both from the same injection.
  • An RI calibration file (.CAL) for your column and oven program, read by read_ri_calibration(). Retention times are instrument-specific; the retention index re-expresses them on a standard scale, which is what lets peaks be matched against library RIs later.
  • Sample metadata from sample_info(): a sample ID, density, and water or methanol content in wt% if present in the matrix. Density anchors the mass balance for internal quantification, and declared water/methanol keeps those out of the compound accounting.
  • For identification: NIST-format library directories and the mspepsearchr package (Windows). Without them everything upstream still runs – deconvolution and quantification work fine; you just get unnamed peaks with interpolated formulas.
  • For reports: openxlsx for the Excel workbook, and the Quarto CLI with LaTeX for the PDF.

Run it

The example we work on here is diesel fuel, with a spike of phenols and octanol (in isopropanol) added. The file names below are simply those in your working directory; on a desktop PC this run takes roughly an hour end to end, most of it per-window deconvolution and library searching.

The NIST-format library directories are supplied through the moosaic.library_path option rather than as an argument – set once, every call in the session uses them (here they point at our local NIST 23 install; adjust to your own).

info <- sample_info(
  "phenols-in-diesel",
  sample_name = "phenols-in-diesel",
  density = 0.85554,
  water_wt_pct = 36e-4 # 36 ppm water
)

res <- process_sample("./data.ms", "./fid.ch", info, ri_cal = "./ONSITE.CAL")

process_sample() reads the two files, aligns the MS to the FID (the mass spectrometer sees each peak a few seconds late), deconvolves every detected FID window into pure components, searches the library for each one, and quantifies with the internal (Polyarc) style so the amounts total 100 wt% of the sample density. The result is a moosaic_result; everything downstream reads from it.

Reading the results

The peak table is what you would hand to someone: one row per quantified peak in retention-time order, from total_compound_table(). Columns worth knowing: Amount (ug/mL) is the Polyarc amount; Target or Relative says how it was obtained – directly as a target, or relative to the reference peak; MS Match Score and Final Score are the library match factor on its 0–1000 scale with and without the RI and element penalties applied. Peaks that were not identified have NA scores and an interpolated formula.

tbl <- total_compound_table(res)
#> Error:
#> ! object 'res' not found
tbl[!is.na(tbl$`Compound Formula`), ]
#> Error:
#> ! object 'tbl' not found

Behind the peaks, components_to_tibble() has one row per pure component the ALS fit found in each window: fitted areas, the fid_ms_ratio, and explained_variance – values near 1 mean the component’s profile and spectrum reconstruct that window well. This is where you would go to inspect a suspicious deconvolution.

comp <- components_to_tibble(res)
#> Error:
#> ! object 'res' not found
head(comp[, setdiff(names(comp), c("chromatogram", "spectrum"))])
#> Error:
#> ! object 'comp' not found

With internal quantification the peak amounts normalise to a total of 100 wt%:

sum(res$peaks$wt_pct)
#> Error:
#> ! object 'res' not found

Reports

write_excel_report() writes a two-sheet workbook – a Total Compound Report (sample header plus the peak table above) and a Summary Report (family and element balances, QC numbers, footnotes); write_pdf_report() renders the bundled Quarto template with the same content minus the analyst-only columns. Pass an output path as shown, or let each function name the file from your project code and sample ID. Both packages are Suggests, so install openxlsx / quarto to produce these yourself.

write_excel_report(res, "report.xlsx")
#> Loading required namespace: openxlsx
#> Error:
#> ! object 'res' not found
write_pdf_report(res, "report.pdf")
#> Error:
#> ! object 'res' not found
list.files(pattern = "^report\\.(xlsx|pdf)$")
#> character(0)
First page of the PDF report.

Where to go next

  • Every tunable option is documented in the options vignette.
  • The stage functions (read_experiment(), align_detectors(), deconvolve_run(), process_window(), fit_window()) let you intervene on individual windows – for instance, to re-fit one whose rank confidence came out low; see their help pages.
